messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA experts,

I am working on network meta-analysis models with INLA (as an extension of this paper: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26360927)

So far, I obtained very similar results with INLA compared to MCMC (via JAGS) with several datasets. However, with one dataset, one of the parameter estimate (d14) gave very different result compared to MCMC. Then I tried strategy = "laplace", it gave median estimates more closer to MCMC, however posterior densities seem very strange. I attached the posterior densities (Marginal_posteriors.pdf).  Also I attached BUGS code (and R code) and model is a fixed effect network meta-analysis model.

Moreover, MCMC implementation shows that there is high autocorrelation of this parameter. Other thing is there is not much information on that particular parameter.

What could be possible explanation of this situation that simplified laplace and laplace strategies gave very different results? and how can I overcome it?

Thank you very much for your time,

Best,

Burak

messages.subject_clean: possible numerical issues with hurdle model?
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA experts,

I am fitting a zero hurdle model with the following features:
binomial and gamma likelihoods
iid error terms on each observation and on two spatially aggregate groups
control.inla = list(correct = TRUE, correct.factor = 10) --> my attempt to address issues with the combination of the binomial likelihood and iid error terms
4 consecutive empirical bayes models to cool down the diagonal parameter from 1000-100-10-1 into the main model, where diagonal = 0 (control.mode = list(result = eb_modelName, restart = TRUE) --> to improve starting values for full INLA method
prior precision = 1 for the fixed coefficients and intercept --> increased precision to get around NaN values in the DIC in previous runs of the model
tolerance = 1e-6
I've noticed some odd things in the model output and I am wondering if this may point to possible numerical issues:
a handful of the fitted values from the binomial component of the model produce mode = NaN although numerical values are reported for the mean, standard deviation, and other quantiles
for one of the observations with where the binomial fitted value mode was NaN, there is a really large fitted value for the gamma component of the model -- orders of magnitude larger than the observed value. The standard deviation is also very large.
These symptoms were consistent when I tried running models with a subset of the observations and with fewer covariates.

Does anyone have thoughts on what might cause these symptoms? Should I be concerned about the validity of the model output?

Regards,
Elizabeth

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I'm having trouble figuring the variance of my non-spatial, non-temporal components in my model. I'm using a variation of the code used in Musenge et al. 2013, Bayesian analysis of zero inflated spatiotemporal HIV/TB child mortality data through the INLA and SPDE approaches: Applied to data observed between 1992 and 2010 in rural North East South Africa.

They do their temporal aspect a little differently than the Cameletti 2012 example, simply specifying the AR1 as another random effect rather than using the "Group" functionality to include it in the SPDE. (Is this still correct?)

Here is an example of my code:

loc<-cbind(DataWithDaymet$Long,DataWithDaymet$Lat) #Stores the lat/longs of each observation site
bnd<-inla.nonconvex.hull(loc,convex=0.1) #Makes a nonconvex hull around the points rather than the spatial extent of the island
mesh<-inla.mesh.2d(boundary=bnd, cutoff=0.05, max.edge=c(0.1,0.2))

#Creating the INLA with 1 week weather lag
A <-inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc)
spde<-inla.spde2.matern(mesh,alpha=2)
formula<-Result ~ -1 + SepCt + NDVI + OpWat + DevLow + WWet+ EHWet + PrcpL1 + TavgL1 + f(spatial, model=spde) + f(Week, model= "ar1")
vars<-DataWithDaymet[,c(5,7,8,9,10,15,16,32,39)] #Week is included here, in Vars
vars[,(1:9)]<- sapply(vars[,(1:9)],as.numeric)
vars[,2:9]<-scale(vars)[,2:9] #Scaling by mean and SD
stk<-inla.stack(data=list(Result=DataWithDaymet$Result),A=list(A,1),effect=list(list(spatial=1:spde$n.spde),data.frame(vars)))
r<-inla(formula, family="zeroinflatedbinomial1", control.family=list(link="logit"), data=inla.stack.data(stk), control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk)),control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))
summary(r)

and here is an example of the output:

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-tzGFC444dsU/V-Po7efjwNI/AAAAAAAACdU/nRTRbWd54cc4Og5th7YrMUGpRR9LRXMEQCLcB/s1600/INLA_Spatiotemp_Result.PNG>

I can see how to calculate tau and kappa from the thetas, and how to use those to obtain sigma^2 for the spatial component. However, I don't see the "Precision for the Gaussian observations" that is used in the Cameletti paper to obtain the variance. Am I doing something wrong?

Thanks very much,

Mark Myer

Hi,

I think that I finally figured out what was the problem.
Actually, even after updating the packages, the problem still persisted. However, after looking to your figure, its resolution was much better than mine. Thus, I thought that the problem could be due the resolution of the polygon.
Knowing that the argument ''worldHires'' in the map() function provides maps with higher resolution than the ''world'' argument, I tryed to draw the polygon according this specific argument. Although my figure still looks different than yours (see attaced file), the code finally works. Despite of this, I had to improve your code a little bit and maybe you want to update it for the next time. Here are the codelines that I used:

data("worldHiresMapEnv")

nor_coast_poly <- map("worldHires", "norway", fill=TRUE, col="transparent",
                      plot=FALSE, ylim=c(58,72))
nor_coast_poly$names
IDs <- sapply(strsplit(nor_coast_poly$names, ":"), function(x) x[1])
nor_coast_poly_sp <- map2SpatialPolygons(nor_coast_poly, IDs=IDs,
                                         proj4string=CRS("+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84"))
# - copy-paste ended

## We are interested here in a small part of the Norwegian coast
# - it is important not to use a polygon for the whole Norwegian cost
# - limit the polygon to where you have data
# - this is to keep the mesh small
# - a too large mesh leads to a very slow algorithm!

loc3 = matrix(c(4,60.6, 8,60.6, 4,61.5, 8,61.5), 4, 2, byrow = T)
# - this is set to give the right extent of the mesh
# - you can use data locations instead
# - a bit extra offset will be added by the mesh function

square = bakka.square.polygon(xlim=range(loc3[ ,1]), ylim=range(loc3[ ,2]), ret.SP = T)
# - This is the study area
# - Assumption: you are interested in fitting and/or predicting locations inside here
# - You only care about the water area, since land is a barrier

square@proj4string=nor_coast_poly_sp@proj4string

poly3 = gIntersection(nor_coast_poly_sp, square)

Thank you very much for your help!

Best regards,

Marie

messages.subject: Unexpected flat maps
messages.body_plain:
Hello INLA experts!

We have been working with some disease mapping models in an extensive study in the Valencian Region (Spain) and have found some results that we find a bit puzzling. We have been fitting the BYM proposal for a lot of diseases and in occasions we have found some striking flat maps that we considered unreliable. For checking this, we have further fitted those same models in WinBUGS and we have found that the something weird was happening in those results. At least the maps from WinBUGS differed sometimes substantially from those in INLA.

We are attaching a Markdown document (https://drive.google.com/open?id=0BwbigALl4QRYMVd3Y2hWeWNVNVk) with a clear example of what we are referring to. At the beginning of the document you will find the code used for fitting the models. We have fitted this for Asthma for different periods of time. You will see that for shorter periods INLA results are markedly different from those in WinBUGS. At the beginning they are flat and they progressively resemble those in WinBUGS when the number of periods is growing. WinBUGS results from the very beginning resemble the results obtained with longer periods. At the end of the document you will also find a graph with the posterior mean of the log-precisions (for both random effects in BYM) for both WinBUGS and INLA runs. They are markedly different, mainly for the heterogeneous random effects. For the shorter periods both log-precision estimates go to the same value and this value does not change for the heterogeneous effect although the data are different. Surprisingly, for other datasets (pancreatic cancer) we have found both posterior distributions to converge to exactly these same values. Moreover, we have changed the starting point in INLA for these values ( c(1,1), c(2,2) or c(10, 10)) and we have found that regardless this initial value, the trace of these posterior means converge to the values displayed at the markdown document. So the posterior mean does not get stuck at these values from the very starting point of the INLA iterative algorithm. On the contrary they do converge to the values pointed out.

You will see at our document that we have used a uniform prior distribution on the positive real line for the standard deviations since this is the usual choice that we make. But we have also tried a Cauchy prior on the sd as also suggested in the literature and already implemented in INLA and we get the same results. We have also tried with the different approximations used in INLA, such as simplified Laplace, but nothing changes. As mentioned, we have also found this issue with other diseases like pancreatic cancer which present more cases than asthma:

2000 --> 414 cases

2000-2003 --> 1646 cases

2000-2006 --> 2971 cases

2000-2009 --> 4501 cases

2000-20012 --> 6356 cases

2000-2014 --> 7647 cases

Do you have any idea about what could be happening here? Why INLA patterns don’t appear until the 2nd or 3rd maps and WinBUGS detect a pattern first? If uniform priors on the sd does not favour flat maps, why do INLA returns flat maps when little information is available (this is not what the prior would be saying)? Are we missing out something?

Thanks for your help.

Hèctor

these are kind of special models made for a spesific purpose and not
ment to be of public use

if you look at inla.doc("zeroinf")

component it is from. in these likelihoods, that probability is set to

if you want the 'type1' version, then you cannot use this setup, as
observing y=0 you do not know which component it came from.

for continous response this is particular easy, as you can never
observe y==0  by chance.

let me know if you have further questions

messages.body_plain:
Hello Håvard,

Thanks for your answer. We already took into account that the "island" at the left of our map could be a problem so the adjacency matrix had artificially linked that island to the mainland by means of putting as adjacent those of their municipalities which are closer.

Yesterday we performed some tests with different diseases and configurations. The problem seems to be solved by changing the place of the priors specification, as you commented in your reply. We weren't aware that the prior specifications could not worked if they were placed out of the f() functions. Is this documented at any place? since this was right long before, is this right?

Finally, our examples make evident the problems that could entail the use of "non-informative" Gamma priors on the precisions of the BYM model. Namely, for scarcer data the posterior mean goes straight to the prior mean of the "non-informative" prior distribution which does not happen with the uniform distribution on the sd. Taking results of this kind into account, have you thought on changing the default prior distributions for those precisions to less dangerous proposals (such as the uniform prior on the sds)? In my opinion this would not be a foolish idea.

Best regards,
Hèctor
